title: Open-pit mine benches: one cone etch exposes every tier
idea: Borrowed from open-pit mining benches: instead of 3D-NAND-style resist-trim staircases (dozens of litho/trim cycles), one tapered isotropic etch cuts a conical pit through the whole 3D DRAM tier stack so every wordline tier surfaces as a concentric ring on the pit wall. Contacts land on the rings at radii set by cone angle and tier thickness, using a single contact mask.
why: Attacks 3D DRAM mask/capital cost (facts 2,4): replaces ~N/2 trim cycles with one etch; ring contacts wrap around the pit so staircase area falls ~3x and staircase process cost ~80% at 64+ tiers.

title: Skyscraper sky lobbies: tier-local sense amps every 16 tiers
idea: Adapted from supertall-building sky lobbies (express elevator to a lobby, local elevators onward): long vertical bitlines in a 3D DRAM stack are cut into 16-tier segments, each ending at a 'sky lobby' tier holding oxide-TFT local sense amps that drive a low-swing express global bitline down to CMOS.
why: Bitline capacitance seen per sense drops ~8x, so Cs can shrink from ~5 fF to <1 fF with the same margin (fact 1) and stacks can exceed 100 tiers without a high-AR capacitor (fact 2).

title: Cross-laminated timber: each conductor plane serves two tiers
idea: Like CLT boards glued with alternating grain, conductor planes alternate X/Y orientation: each plane is the bitline of the tier below and, through a thin gate dielectric, the gate/wordline of the tier above, with an oxide-semiconductor cell at every crossing.
why: Halves deposition/etch layers per tier (~4 to ~2), cutting stack height and per-tier cost ~40% and pulling the 26-tier break-even (fact 2) toward ~15 tiers.

title: Image-sensor pixel bonding: one sense amp per 64 cells
idea: Borrowed from stacked CMOS image sensors with pixel-level Cu-Cu hybrid bonds and per-pixel ADCs: bond the array wafer face-to-face to a logic wafer at sub-1 um pitch so every 64-cell micro-bitline lands on its own sense amp, eliminating long bitlines entirely.
why: Bitline capacitance falls from ~50-80 fF to ~2 fF, so Cs can drop to ~0.5 fF (no 70:1 pillar, fact 1), read energy ~10x lower, and periphery leaves the array die (fact 7).

title: Zipper teeth: capacitor meshes together at the hybrid-bond interface
idea: Like interlocking zipper teeth, each of two bonded wafers carries half of an interdigitated fin capacitor (storage-node fins on the transistor wafer, plate fins on the top wafer), both pre-coated with high-k; hybrid bonding meshes them into a capacitor of double height with no single high-AR etch.
why: Splits the 60-75:1 pillar etch (fact 1) into two ~35:1 etches; ~2x electrode area at equal etch difficulty, ~5-8 fF at relaxed aspect ratio.

title: CCD imager registers: vertical charge-shift strings replace capacitors
idea: Adapted from CCD image sensors: a 3D gate stack wrapped around a vertical silicon or oxide-semiconductor channel stores bits as charge packets in potential wells under each gate tier; a read clocks packets down the string to a floating-diffusion sense node at the base, like a CCD vertical register.
why: Removes both 3D blockers, the capacitor and the lateral transistor (fact 2); ~4F2/N per bit with NAND-like one-litho-for-all-tiers cost; trade-off ~50-100 ns serial shift for 32-tier strings.

title: Corrugated cardboard flutes: tiers deposited over sinusoidal templates
idea: Borrowed from corrugated board, where a fluted middle sheet multiplies stiffness and surface: etch a shallow sinusoidal corrugation into the base, then deposit the 3D tier stack so every horizontal tier and its lateral capacitor follow the wave, multiplying electrode area without deep etches.
why: Lateral 3D capacitors gain ~2.5-3x area (facts 1-2) using only shallow features, e.g. Cs ~1.5 to ~4 fF per horizontal cell.

title: Aerospace honeycomb: hex-packed cells with three 120-degree line sets
idea: Adapted from honeycomb sandwich cores: vertical-channel cells sit on a hexagonal close-packed lattice addressed by three line families at 120 degrees (wordline, bitline, plate-select), with a cell chosen by coincidence of two of them.
why: Hex packing gives ~3.5F2 vs 4F2 square and 6F2 today (fact 4), ~15% more bits per litho area, plus isotropic support that resists tall-pillar collapse.

title: Phased-array radar timing: colliding pulses select the wordline segment
idea: Borrowed from radar/ultrasound beam steering: a long tier wordline is driven as a transmission line from both ends with two sub-threshold pulses timed to superpose above threshold only at the target segment, selecting it without any per-segment decoder.
why: Deletes local wordline decoders and drivers in 3D stacks (fact 7, periphery ~49%), periphery area ~-30%; requires ps-level timing control.

title: Roof shingles: inclined lateral capacitors overlap neighbor footprints
idea: Like overlapping roof shingles, each lateral capacitor in a 3D stack is built on a slant, climbing one tier over its length, so it extends beneath the next cell's footprint without colliding; the slant comes from an inclined sacrificial ramp cut by tilted ion-beam etch.
why: Doubles capacitor length per lateral pitch in 3D DRAM (facts 1-2), ~2x Cs without raising tier pitch.

title: Tantalum capacitor powder metallurgy: sintered nanosponge storage electrode
idea: Adapted from solid tantalum capacitor anodes (pressed, sintered powder with enormous internal area): fill each storage-node cavity with a sintered TiN/Ru nanoparticle sponge, then ALD high-k and the plate electrode through its open pores.
why: Surface enhancement ~5-10x per volume lets a 20:1 cavity match a 70:1 pillar (fact 1), relieving high-AR etch and pattern collapse.

title: Precast concrete: test each crystalline tier before stacking it
idea: Like precast panels cured and inspected off-site, each single-crystal DRAM tier is built on a donor, wafer-tested, and only then transferred by hydrogen smart-cut onto the stack, with bad sub-arrays remapped before the next tier is added.
why: Monocrystalline lateral transistors in every tier (facts 2,3: tighter leakage tail) and stack yield that does not compound per tier, making 26+ tiers economic.

title: Cable TV frequency multiplexing reads eight tiers on one line
idea: Borrowed from FDM in cable TV: each tier's cell group couples to a shared vertical line through an on-tier LC or ring resonator with a distinct frequency; a multi-tone read pulse interrogates 8 tiers at once and the sense chain separates them by frequency.
why: Cuts vertical bitlines and sense amps per footprint ~8x in 3D stacks (fact 7); signal levels are the open risk.

title: Cellular frequency reuse: four-color tier activation shares drivers
idea: Adapted from cellular frequency-reuse coloring: tiers and subarrays are assigned four 'colors' and neighboring same-color regions never activate together, so one wordline-driver bank serves four tiers in rotation and aggressor rows are never adjacent to active victims.
why: Wordline driver count ~4x lower in 3D stacks (fact 7) and inter-tier row-hammer coupling bounded by construction (fact 9).

title: LTPS display lasers crystallize silicon for every 3D tier
idea: Borrowed from LTPS phone-display backplanes: each 3D tier receives low-temperature amorphous Si that is melted and recrystallized by line-beam excimer laser pulses too short to heat the tiers below, yielding large-grain lateral transistors tier by tier.
why: Silicon-class mobility (~10x IGZO drive) for monolithic 3D lateral transistors without high-temperature epi (fact 2); the laser tools already exist at Gen-6 scale.

title: Termite-mound chimneys: heat-pipe pillars threaded through the stack
idea: Adapted from termite-mound ventilation shafts: every 64th vertical bitline slot in a DRAM-on-logic stack becomes a Cu/diamond 'chimney' pillar tying all tiers to a top heat spreader, holding every tier within ~5 C of the coolant.
why: Retention roughly halves per ~10 C, so cooler tiers cut refresh power ~2-4x (fact 3) and allow DRAM stacked directly on hot accelerators (fact 5).

title: ISO shipping-container standard for interchangeable memory tiers
idea: Like the ISO container standard, publish an open 'memory brick' spec: fixed 1 um hybrid-bond grid, power/signal pin map, test hooks and thickness, so any vendor's array tier or logic base stacks with any other.
why: Breaks HBM's vertically integrated stack (fact 6), lets U.S. fabs make bases or tiers separately, and pools capacity across many fabs; stack NRE down ~50%.

title: Blu-ray layer focus: threshold-window gates select tiers by voltage
idea: Borrowed from multilayer optical discs where focus depth picks the layer: each tier's access transistor has two series gates on two shared vertical lines, with thresholds graded up the stack on one and down on the other, so voltage level k on both turns on only tier k, with no per-tier staircase contact.
why: Removes staircase contacts and per-tier drivers for ~8 tiers per gate pair (facts 2,7); staircase area ~-80%.

title: Hard-disk TDMR: joint bitline sensing cancels neighbor crosstalk
idea: Adapted from two-dimensional magnetic recording, where multiple readers cancel inter-track interference: sense amps resolve neighboring bitline pairs jointly and subtract a calibrated coupling term, letting bitline pitch go below today's coupling limit.
why: Bitline pitch ~25-30% tighter at the same litho (fact 4), cost per bit ~-20%, and tolerance for denser 3D pitches.

title: Multilateral oil wells: six lateral cells branch from one hole
idea: Borrowed from multilateral drilling, where one vertical well feeds many horizontal laterals: each vertical bitline hole in a 3D stack is recessed in six directions per tier by a crystallographic wet etch, forming six lateral cells in a star around one vertical line.
why: Vertical holes per bit fall ~3x vs two-sided designs, ~2x 3D bit density per footprint (fact 2).

title: Coaxial cable: grounded sleeves around every vertical bitline
idea: Adapted from coax: each vertical bitline in a 3D array is wrapped in a thin grounded metal sleeve over low-k, trading ~20% more self-capacitance for near-zero coupling to neighbor bitlines and plates.
why: Coupling noise ~-80% allows open-bitline 4F2 3D arrays without folded/twisted schemes and smaller sense margins (fact 1).

title: LNG cryogenic logistics: 77 K racks enable capacitor-less tiers
idea: Borrowed from LNG handling: memory sleds run immersed in liquid nitrogen, where subthreshold leakage falls by many orders of magnitude, so a bare floating node in a 3D tier holds charge for seconds to hours with no capacitor at all.
why: Removes the capacitor (facts 1-2) and nearly all refresh (fact 3); wire resistance drops ~6x; cooling overhead ~10-20% of saved power.

title: Duplex printing: DRAM arrays on both faces of one wafer
idea: Adapted from duplex printing and logic backside power delivery: build the array on the front, bond to a carrier, thin, and build a second array on the backside of the same silicon, sharing periphery through nano-TSVs in the middle.
why: Roughly doubles bits per wafer start while sharing substrate and periphery, ~1.6x lower cost per bit.

title: LCD panel fabs make DRAM by the square meter on glass
idea: Adapted from TFT-LCD backplanes (an LCD pixel is literally a 1T1C DRAM cell): run 1T1C oxide-TFT arrays on 3 m x 3 m Gen-10.5 glass in idle display fabs, reach ~375 nm features with self-aligned quadruple spacers, and stack 8 TFT tiers; accept 200-500 ns access and a heavy refresh budget.
why: ~1.2 Mb/mm2 per tier x 8 tiers x 9 m2 is ~10 TB per panel for ~$1-2k, about $0.1-0.2/GB, ~50-100x below 2026 DRAM; no EUV, no quartz crucibles.

title: Millefiori glass canes: thermally draw a macro preform into nanocells
idea: Borrowed from millefiori glass and optical-fiber preform drawing: assemble a centimeter-scale preform whose cross-section holds semiconducting glass, metal and dielectric regions forming a cell row, thermally draw it ~10,000x into kilometers of fiber, then slice, bundle and bond cross-sections as arrays with no lithography.
why: Pattern is made once at mm scale and replicated at km/hour; capital per bit ~1/100 of a fab; trade-offs: chalcogenide/oxide-glass devices, ~1 us access, coarse yield.

title: Battery jelly-roll winding: wind single-tier DRAM foil into cylinders
idea: Adapted from Li-ion jelly-roll cells: imprint a single-tier oxide-TFT array on a 5 um polyimide web at roll speed, then wind ~1,000 turns into a cylinder whose battery-style edge tabs bring segmented bitlines and wordlines out to a bonded controller.
why: Volume density comes from winding, not tier deposition; web processing at ~$5-10/m2 x 1,000 turns gives TB per cylinder near $0.05-0.1/GB; trade-offs: microsecond access, module-sized form factor.

title: Snack-bag web metallizers vacuum-coat 128-tier stacks by the kilometer
idea: Borrowed from roll-to-roll metallizers that coat packaging film at ~1,000 m/min: deposit 128 alternating Mo/SiOx wordline/insulator layers on a heat-tolerant web in multi-drum passes, laminate the stack onto a CMOS wafer, then one hole etch plus ALD finishes vertical-channel gain cells.
why: Tier-stack deposition is a dominant 3D cost; web coating is ~100x cheaper per m2, and with one mask for all tiers the path reaches ~$0.1/GB; trade-offs: lamination voids, lower tier quality, refresh-heavy cells.

title: DVD replication: molded substrates carry all cell topography
idea: Adapted from DVD/Blu-ray replication (a nanostructured disc molded every ~3 s from one nickel stamper): mold glass-ceramic or high-Tg substrates that already contain capacitor wells, gate trenches and contact steps, then conformally coat electrode, high-k, IGZO and metal and planarize, so array geometry needs no lithography.
why: Collapses 5-7 EUV layers and their etches (fact 4) into one molding amortized over ~10^5 parts, ~100x lower patterning cost per GB; trade-offs: ~40 nm features, low-temperature materials, slower cells.

title: Anodized aluminum pores self-assemble the capacitor forest without etch
idea: Borrowed from architectural aluminum anodizing: sputter 3 um of Al over the access-transistor array, imprint shallow dimples at cell sites, and anodize so hexagonal pores self-align to them at ~100:1 aspect ratio; line the pores with TiN/high-k/TiN to form every capacitor without plasma etch or EUV.
why: A wet bath replaces the hardest high-AR etch module and its masks (facts 1,4), capacitor module cost ~-95%; with a relaxed ~30 nm EUV-free periphery it is a core piece of a 100x cost path.

title: Leaky flash: 3D NAND fabs build volatile charge-trap DRAM
idea: Adapted from 3D NAND (already ~$0.05/GB): keep the 200+ tier charge-trap string but thin the tunnel oxide to ~1.5 nm direct-tunneling so writes take ~10-50 ns at ~4 V, retention drops to ~1 s and endurance rises beyond 10^12; read through NAND page buffers and refresh each second, fronted by an SRAM cache.
why: Inherits NAND's per-bit cost (~100x below DRAM) and U.S.-buildable toolsets; trade-offs: 100-300 ns page-random reads and page-granular access.

title: Optical-disc error correction lets arrays ship with 1% dead cells
idea: Borrowed from CDs and Blu-ray, which ship with defects and rely on interleaved Reed-Solomon/LDPC: design arrays with soft-decision sensing and ~25% parity so up to 1% dead or weak-retention cells are absorbed, eliminating laser repair and per-cell screening.
why: The enabler that makes 100x-cheap processes (panels, imprint, 200+ tiers) sellable: effective yield on 100-tier stacks rises from ~30% to ~95%, a ~3x lever inside the 100x stack-up.

title: Used-ship market: depreciated 200 mm fabs build deep tier stacks
idea: Like shipping firms buying used vessels, acquire fully depreciated 65-180 nm 200 mm fabs and run only deposition-heavy 256-tier vertical stacks at ~90 nm pitch (one KrF/i-line litho per 64 tiers), bonding a thin modern logic base later.
why: Depreciation (~55% of wafer cost, fact 4) goes to ~zero while 256 tiers at 90 nm still give ~8 Gb/mm2; ~30-100x lower cost per bit; trade-offs: big die, ~200 ns latency.

title: Shingled-recording discipline: overlapping cells written in sequential bands
idea: Adapted from SMR hard drives, which overlap tracks and require sequential zone writes: adjacent storage nodes along a row share partially overlapping electrodes with no isolation, and a band is written in order so each write fixes the trailing cell's charge; reads remain random.
why: Removing isolation spacing gives ~2-3F2 cells, ~2-3x density (fact 4); stacked in tiers this is a 100x path for read-mostly AI weights and KV cache; trade-off: band-granular writes.

title: Pulse electroplating grows a 200-layer wordline stack in one bath
idea: Borrowed from compositionally modulated multilayer electroplating: plate a 200-period Cu/Ni superlattice from one bath by switching potential, selectively recess one metal and backfill oxide, forming the 3D wordline stack without CVD tungsten.
why: Plating costs ~1/100 of CVD/ALD per layer and avoids tungsten (China ~80%); stack deposition cost ~-95%; trade-offs: barrier liners, uniformity at the wafer edge.

title: Grid surge-arrester zinc-oxide varistors select crossbar DRAM capacitors
idea: Adapted from power-grid metal-oxide surge arresters, whose ZnO grain boundaries conduct ~10^10x more above a knee voltage: stack 8 decks of 1-selector-1-capacitor crossbars where a nanograin ZnO-Bi2O3 varistor film isolates each capacitor below half-select voltage, 2 masks per deck.
why: Transistor-free crossbar decks reach ~4F2/8 per bit at a fraction of DRAM process cost, ~100x cheaper per GB; trade-offs: ~ms retention needing aggressive refresh, high write voltages.

title: Turbine-blade eutectic solidification grows built-in vertical nanorod plates
idea: Borrowed from directionally solidified eutectic alloys used in turbine blades: solidify a Si-TaSi2 eutectic ingot so billions of aligned metallic TaSi2 nanorods run through monocrystalline Si, then slice wafers in which each rod is a ready-made vertical capacitor plate or buried bitline, with cells formed around them by one mask.
why: Self-organized vertical conductors replace high-AR etch and fill (facts 1,4); a ~100x path if fast growth brings rod pitch near ~100 nm; trade-off: irregular lattice needs per-die mapping.

title: Diffraction-grating interference lithography patterns periodic arrays maskless
idea: Adapted from holographic diffraction-grating production: since cell arrays are periodic, expose the whole array with two- or three-beam 193 nm immersion interference (~40 nm half-pitch, no mask, no EUV) and use cheap conventional litho only for array edges and periphery.
why: Interference tools cost ~1/20 of a scanner and expose a wafer in seconds; combined with 3D tiers, patterning cost per bit ~-95% (fact 4) toward 100x per GB.

title: Veneer slicing: deposit layers, slice block, get 10 nm lines
idea: Borrowed from wood-veneer slicing and nanoskiving: deposit 500 alternating 10 nm metal/oxide layers as a thick block, slice it perpendicular with a diamond microtome into thin slabs, and lay the slabs flat so the cut face exposes 10 nm lines whose pitch is set by deposition, not litho; cross two slabs for a crosspoint array.
why: Sub-10 nm wordline/bitline gratings without EUV (fact 4), patterning cost ~1/100; trade-offs: slab registration, needs a crosspoint-compatible gain cell or selector.

title: Williams-tube revival: field-emitter arrays write charge on bare film
idea: Adapted from the 1940s CRT Williams-tube memory and field-emission displays: a CMOS-driven field-emitter tip array (one tip per ~1,000 bits) sits ~1 um above an unpatterned dielectric storage film in vacuum; each tip deflects its micro-beam to deposit charge spots and reads them by secondary-emission current.
why: The storage film costs cents per wafer and needs no transistors, wires or litho; only the tip array is patterned at relaxed pitch, ~100x lower cost per bit in principle; trade-offs: vacuum package, 100 ns-1 us access, spot drift needing refresh.

title: Engine remanufacturing: harvest and restack DRAM dies from e-waste
idea: Like remanufactured engines and toner cartridges: buy scrapped server DIMMs by the ton, debond and retest the dies, then edge-stack or hybrid-bond 8-16 known-good dies onto a new logic base die with fresh interface and strong ECC, sold as certified 'reman' capacity memory.
why: Harvested die cost approaches scrap value (~$0.05-0.2/GB), so restacked modules can be ~30-100x cheaper per GB than new 2026 contract DRAM; trade-offs: older densities, mixed speed bins, shorter warranty.

title: Image-sensor ramp ADCs read sixteen charge levels per cell
idea: Borrowed from CMOS image sensors, whose column-parallel single-slope ADCs digitize thousands of pixels with one shared ramp: each bitline gets a tiny comparator-counter so a cell holds 16 charge levels (4 bits), written by ramp-and-stop and digitally restored on every read.
why: 4 bits/cell lets a 40 nm ArF-dry, EUV-free array at ~1/5 the wafer cost match today's density; with 16 stacked tiers cost per GB falls ~100x; trade-offs: ~200 ns reads, more frequent refresh.

title: Film-projector token ring replaces decoders for CMOS-free tiles
idea: Adapted from film projectors that advance one frame per sprocket pulse: each 1 Mb tile selects rows with a token passed along an in-array oxide-TFT shift register and streams columns out a shift-register row buffer, so the tile has no address decoders and can be built entirely from TFTs on glass or foil.
why: Periphery shrinks from ~49% of die to ~5% (fact 7) and CMOS leaves the array substrate, enabling panel- or roll-built memory near $0.1/GB; trade-off: sequential row walks (~1 us worst case) hidden by a cache.

title: Solar chemical-bath deposition grows channels in thousand-wafer tanks
idea: Borrowed from thin-film solar, where CdS/ZnO buffer layers grow from warm aqueous baths in huge batches: grow the ZnO/InZnO channel and Al2O3 gate liner inside 256-tier vertical holes by self-limiting chemical bath deposition, ~1,000 wafers per tank instead of single-wafer ALD.
why: ALD/CVD dominates 3D memory capex; a ~$1M bath line replaces ~$100M of ALD, cutting the channel module ~100x and pulling total cost per GB toward the 100x target; trade-offs: lower mobility, more refresh.

title: Nanotube-forest growth: grow vertical channels instead of etching holes
idea: Adapted from carbon-nanotube forest growth, where catalyst dots sprout aligned tubes millimeters tall: place catalyst at cell sites, grow vertical Si or oxide-semiconductor nanowires to ~5 um by VLS, then build the tier stack around them with low-temperature conformal fills, so no 70:1 hole etch is ever needed.
why: High-AR hole etch and its tools are among the costliest 3D steps (facts 2,4); 100-wafer growth batches cut this module ~50x; misaligned wires handled by redundancy.

title: Self-stratifying paint: one coat separates into fifty tier layers
idea: Borrowed from self-stratifying industrial coatings that split into primer and topcoat in one application: spin a block-copolymer plus metal-oxide-precursor blend that phase-separates into ~50 parallel lamellae, then UV-ozone convert and anneal it into alternating conductive-oxide and insulating-oxide tiers for a vertical gain-cell stack.
why: One coat-and-bake replaces ~100 CVD steps for a 50-tier stack, aiming at ~100x lower stack cost; trade-off: oxide-electrode resistance limits access to hundreds of ns.

title: Telephone line concentrators: one sense amp serves 1024 bitlines
idea: Adapted from telephone line concentrators where many subscribers share few trunks: a tree of oxide-TFT pass switches inside the array tiers lets 1,024 bitlines share one CMOS sense amp, and each cell is an active gain cell so it can drive the long shared path instead of sharing tiny charge.
why: Sense-amp and periphery area fall ~95% (fact 7), collapsing CMOS area per GB so arrays stack on a cheap base, ~100x cost cut with tier stacking; trade-off: ~1 us per full row, fine for bulk capacity.
